title: How Can a Man Be Just Before God? Bildad's Last Word
summary: In the shortest speech in the book, Bildad praises God's dominion and the order he keeps in the heavens, where his armies cannot be counted and his light rises on everyone. If even the moon and stars are not pure in God's sight, he asks, how can a human being, a mere maggot and worm, be righteous before him?
story: This is the last time any of Job's three friends speaks. The first two cycles of speeches each had three speakers; in the third cycle Eliphaz gave a full speech (chapter 22), Bildad gives only these six verses, and Zophar says nothing at all. The friends are running out of arguments. They have described the fate of the wicked, called Job to repent, and finally accused him of specific crimes, and nothing has moved him. Bildad falls back on the one point no one disputes: God is great and humans are small. Job agreed with this long ago (9:2), so Bildad's speech adds nothing new. Job will answer in chapter 26 and then speak without interruption through chapter 31, after which a new speaker, Elihu, appears (chapters 32 to 37).
historical:
Bildad is called the Shuhite (verse 1), which probably links him with Shuah, one of the sons Abraham had by Keturah (Genesis 25:2). The descendants of Keturah are associated with the Arabian and Transjordanian regions east of Israel, which fits the book's setting in Uz among the people of the East. Beyond that, nothing is known of Bildad outside this book.

His speech reflects a common ancient Near Eastern picture of the heavens as the realm of God's court and army. Many surrounding peoples worshiped the moon and stars as gods; the moon god, known as Sin in Mesopotamia, was especially important in cities such as Ur and Harran. Bildad's claim that even the moon and stars are not pure before God (verse 5) quietly places those supposed deities among God's creatures. In Israel's faith they were not gods but lights he made.
cultural:
The troops of verse 2 are the heavenly hosts, the vast armies of angelic beings (and in some texts the stars themselves) that serve God. The title LORD of Hosts, common in the prophets, pictures God as the commander of these armies. The question on whom his light does not rise (verse 3) may refer to the sun, which shines on every land, as a sign of God's reach over all people.

The maggot and the worm (verse 6) were familiar images of decay, associated with rotting food and with the grave (Job has already used them of his own body and of the dead in 7:5, 17:14, and 21:26). The phrase one born of woman (verse 4) is a standard Hebrew way of stressing human frailty and mortality, and Job himself used it at the start of his great lament on human weakness (14:1).
literary: The speech is a short hymn of praise followed by a rhetorical question, in the style of the doxologies found throughout Job and the Psalms. Verses 2-3 celebrate God's power and order in the heavens. Verse 4 poses the central question in two parallel lines: How can a man be just before God? How can one born of woman be pure? Verses 5-6 answer with an argument from the greater to the lesser, a form of reasoning common in Hebrew wisdom: if the brightest things in heaven are not pure before God, how much less a human being. Bildad's question closely repeats what Eliphaz said in 4:17-19 and 15:14-16, and it echoes Job's own words in 9:2. The brevity itself is part of the book's design. The friends' speeches are shrinking, and the conversation is collapsing. Some scholars think part of chapter 26 originally belonged to this speech, a question discussed in the next chapter's note.

outline.t: How can a human being be righteous before God?

doctrines.note: Bildad rightly stresses the vast distance between God's purity and human weakness. Nothing in creation, not even the moon and stars, compares with God's holiness. What he does not say is that this God might draw near to a man in his frailty.

Bildad calls humanity a maggot and a worm. The Bible does describe human beings as frail and mortal, but it also calls them God's image (Genesis 1:27) and only a little lower than heavenly beings (Psalm 8:5). Bildad's anthropology is half the truth.

Bildad's question, how can a man be just before God, is one of the great questions of the Bible. The book of Job raises it without answering it in the friends' terms. The New Testament answers it with the gospel of God's grace: God justifies the ungodly through faith in Christ.

words.note: Tsadaq, to be righteous, to be in the right, or to be justified. In legal contexts it means to be declared innocent. Bildad uses it in verse 4. Job has used the same verb again and again for his hope of vindication, and Bildad's question denies that any human could ever stand in the right before God.

Shalom, peace, wholeness, or well-being. In verse 2 Bildad says God establishes shalom in the heights of heaven, meaning order and harmony among the heavenly powers. Some interpreters hear an allusion to ancient stories of conflict in the heavens, which God has put to rest.
Rimmah, maggot or worm. It is the word for the creatures of decay, used of spoiled manna (Exodus 16:24) and of the grave. Bildad uses it in verse 6 to describe what humans are before God.

Tolea, worm. A near synonym of rimmah, used in parallel with it in verse 6. A form of the same word appears in Psalm 22:6, where the sufferer says he is a worm and not a man, and in Isaiah 41:14, where God addresses Israel as a worm and promises to help it.

christ: Bildad's question, how can a man be just before God, is answered in the New Testament in a way he could not have imagined. Paul argues that no one is righteous by their own works, which Bildad would agree with, but that God himself provides righteousness as a gift, justifying those who believe in Jesus (Romans 3:21-26). Bildad saw only the distance between God and humanity. The gospel proclaims that God closed that distance by becoming human. Psalm 22, which the Gospels connect with the crucifixion, uses the same image Bildad uses, a worm, of a sufferer who is scorned by the people and yet delivered by God. The connection with Job 25 is thematic, not predictive. Bildad calls man a worm to silence him; in Christ, God takes on the lowest place in order to lift humanity up.

hard.q: Is Bildad right that humans are nothing but maggots and worms?
hard.a: Bildad's words contain a truth that Scripture affirms elsewhere: human beings are creatures, frail and mortal, and no one can claim to be pure before a holy God on their own merits. Isaiah 41:14 even calls Israel a worm, though in a context of tender promise. But the Bible's full teaching on humanity is richer than Bildad's. Human beings are made in God's image, crowned with glory and honor (Psalm 8:5), and loved by God. Many interpreters note that Bildad uses God's greatness not to comfort Job but to silence him, as if the distance between God and humanity made Job's complaint meaningless. Others observe that his point is not wrong in itself but is misapplied, since Job has never claimed to be sinless, only innocent of the charges the friends bring. On any reading, Bildad's speech shows how the truth of God's holiness can become a weapon when it is separated from the truth of God's love.

questions: Bildad has nothing new to say, so he falls back on God's greatness and human smallness. When have you seen true statements about God used to end a conversation rather than to help someone?
Bildad asks, “How then can a man be just before God?” How would you answer that question?
Bildad calls humans worms, while Psalm 8 says they are crowned with glory. How do you hold together human frailty and human dignity?
